title: Oregon DA Public Records Order — Crombie-CCSO (Clackamas County)
text:
John S. Foote, District Attorney for Clackamas County
Clackamas County Courthouse, 807 Main Street, Room 7, Oregon City, Oregon 97045
(503) 655-8431, FAX (503) 650-8943, www.co.clackamas.or.us/da/
March 16, 2020
VIA E-MAIL
Noelle Crombie
ncrombie@oregonian.com
RE: Public Records Appeal # 319157
Public Record Holder: Clackamas County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO)
Petitioner: Noelle Crombie
Date of Request: March 13, 2020
Ms. Crombie,
This letter is the District Attorney’s response to your petition, appealing CCSO’s denial
of your request for disclosure of records under the Oregon Public Records Law for material
related to the in-custody death of William A. Grote. The Clackamas County Sheriff, through
Clackamas County Counsel, is asserting the exemption under ORS 192.427, as the report was
prepared for and at the request of the Sheriff. ORS 192.427 states in relevant part:
“In any case in which a person is denied the right to inspect or to receive a copy
of a public record in the custody of an elected official, or in the custody of any
other person but as to which an elected official claims the right to withhold
disclosure, no petition to require disclosure may be filed with the Attorney
General or district attorney, or if a petition is filed it shall not be considered by
the Attorney General or district attorney after a claim of right to withhold
disclosure by an elected official. In such case a person denied the right to inspect
or to receive a copy of a public record may institute proceedings for injunctive or
declaratory relief in the appropriate circuit court, as specified in ORS 192.401
(Records of health professional regulatory boards, Health Licensing Office),
192.411 (Petition to review denial of right to inspect state public record) or
192.415 (Procedure to review denial of right to inspect other public records), and
the Attorney General or district attorney may upon request serve or decline to
serve, in the discretion of the Attorney General or district attorney, as counsel in
such suit for an elected official for which the Attorney General or district attorney
ordinarily serves as counsel. Nothing in this section shall preclude an elected
official from requesting advice from the Attorney General or a district attorney as
to whether a public record should be disclosed.”
As such, our office cannot consider your petition. Thank you and please let me know if
you have any questions.
By
Jeffrey M. Nitschke, OSB # 143986

title: Oregon DA Public Records Order — Marshall (Josephine County)
text:
OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT ATTORNEY
Joshua J. Eastman, District Attorney
Josephine County Courthouse
April 13, 2021 500 NW 6th Street, Dept. 16
Grants Pass, OR 97526
Scott Marshall
541-474-5200 | da@josephinecounty.gov
Republican Party of Josephine County
541 Solitude Lane
Grants Pass, OR 97527
541.244.1468
Smars003@hotmail.com
Annette Sorensen
Josephine County Board of Commissioners
500 NW 6th street, Dept. 6
Grants Pass, OR 97526
541.474.5221
RE: Petition for Review of Public Records Request dated April 8, 2021 RE: Josephine County
Security Plan involving elections
Dear Mr. Marshall and Mrs. Sorensen,
Please let this letter serve as my order regarding the Republican Party of Josephine
County by and through Scott Marshall’s (“Party”) petition for the disclosure of records to the
Josephine County Board of Commissioners (“County”) under ORS 192.415(a).
In Oregon, “[e]very person has the right to inspect any public record of a public body in
this state except as expressly provided by ORS 192.338, 192.345, and 192.355. ORS 192.314. A
public body includes every county and city governing body,” a public record “includes any writing
that contains information relating to the conduct of the public’s business,” and a [w]riting means
handwriting, printing, photographing, and every means of recording. ORS 192.311(4-5).
Oregon Public Records Law is primarily a disclosure law, not a confidentiality law. See
Guard Publishing Co. v. Lane Co. Sch. Dist No. 4J, 310 Or 32 (1990). Importantly, every public
record of a public body is subject to inspection, except as provided by the exemptions
mentioned above. See ORS 192.314(1). In short, the presumption is disclosure, and the
exemptions are viewed narrowly. Id. (“if there is a plausible construction of a statute favoring
disclosure of records that is the construction that prevails”).

In this instance, Party requested a “[c]opy of Josephine County Security Plan specifically,
any part that involves elections.” See Pub. Record Req. In Party’s appeal, Party states that
“[o]pacity in these matters only breeds suspicion that there might be something to hide.”
In this case, County denied Party’s record request and relied solely on ORS 254.074(2).
Most public records exemptions are covered in ORS 192.345 and ORS 192.355. ORS 192.345
outlines a list of records that are exempt from disclosure “unless the public interest requires
disclosure in a particular instance.” ORS 192.345. ORS 192.355 outlines a list of records that
“are exempt from disclosure.” ORS 192.355(42). Specific to this case, ORS 254.074(2) states that
“[a] security plan developed and filed under subsection (1) of this section is confidential and not
subject to disclosure under ORS 192.311 to ORS 192.478.” In addition to the clarity of ORS
254.074 and rather redundantly, ORS 192.355(32) exempts “[a] county election security plan
developed and filed under ORS 254.074.”
In reviewing this request and the public records law generally, the “presumption of
disclosure” is foreclosed by both ORS 254.074(2) and ORS 192.355(32). There are two separate
sections explicitly precluding disclosure of the record requested here and neither of them
contain any balancing provisions (see ORS 192.345 and conditional exemptions). That is, even
viewing the exemption narrowly as required, and understanding the public interest in election
security (both generally and currently) as well as the “opacity” mentioned by Party, ORS
192.355(32) and ORS 254.074(2) are clear. Party’s request is DENIED.
Respectfully,
Josh Eastman
District Attorney

title: Oregon DA Public Records Order — Courier-Sorensen (Josephine County)
text:
OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT ATTORNEY
Joshua J. Eastman, District Attorney
Josephine County Courthouse
March 23, 2021 500 NW 6th Street, Dept. 16
Grants Pass, OR 97526
Shaun Hall
541-474-5200 | da@josephinecounty.gov
Grants Pass Daily Courier
409 SE 7th Street
Grants Pass, OR 97528
541.474.3726; 541.761.6726
shall@thedailycourier.com
Annette Sorensen
Josephine County Board of Commissioners
500 NW 6th street, Dept. 6
Grants Pass, OR 97526
541.474.5221
RE: Petition for Review of Public Records Request dated March 4, 2021 RE: McCafferty Reply to
Board
Dear Mr. Hall and Mrs. Sorensen,
Please let this letter serve as my order regarding the Daily Courier by and through Shaun
Hall’s (“Courier”) petition for the disclosure of records to the Josephine County Board of
Commissioners (“County”) under ORS 192.415(a).
In Oregon, “[e]very person has the right to inspect any public record of a public body in
this state except as expressly provided by ORS 192.338, 192.345, and 192.355. ORS 192.314. A
public body includes every county and city governing body,” a public record “includes any writing
that contains information relating to the conduct of the public’s business,” and a [w]riting means
handwriting, printing, photographing, and every means of recording. ORS 192.311(4-5).
Oregon Public Records Law is primarily a disclosure law, not a confidentiality law. See
Guard Publishing Co. v. Lane Co. Sch. Dist No. 4J, 310 Or 32 (1990). Importantly, every public
record of a public body is subject to inspection, except as provided by the exemptions
mentioned above. See ORS 192.314(1). In short, the presumption is disclosure, and the

exemptions are viewed narrowly. Id. (“if there is a plausible construction of a statute favoring
disclosure of records that is the construction that prevails”).
In this instance, we are dealing with one record, which is a “[r]eply of John McCafferty to
a board request regarding security of the county’s election system.” See Courier’s request,
March 4, 2021. Courier further alleges that “it’s of import because of election fraud concerns.”
As part of the ORS 192.415 process, I have reviewed the record that County provided to
me in this matter. Importantly, “[d]isclosure of a record to the district attorney in compliance
with subsection (1) of this section does not waive any privilege or claim of privilege regarding the
record or its contents.” ORS 192.415(3).
In this case, County denied Courier’s record and relied solely on ORS 192.345(23).
ORS 192.345 outlines a list of records that are exempt from disclosure “unless the public interest
requires disclosure in a particular instance.” ORS 192.345. ORS 192.345(23) conditionally
exempts:
Records or information that would reveal or otherwise identify security measures,
or weakness or potential weaknesses in security measures, taken or recommend
to be taken to protect:
(a) An individual;
(b) Buildings or other property
(c) Information processing, communication or telecommunication systems,
including information contained in the systems; or
(d) Those operations of the Oregon State Lottery the security of which are
subject to study and evaluation under ORS 461.180(6).
ORS 192.345(23) (emphasis added).
As pertinent here, the sole question is whether or not the email from Mr. McCafferty
constitutes “information that would reveal or otherwise identify security measures…taken…to
protect…information processing.” Id. This exemption has been applied to video from secret
surveillance camera locations in a courthouse, because disclosing the video would in turn
identify security measures (locations of hidden cameras) as well as potentially reveal weaknesses
(locations not covered by hidden cameras) of security measures within the courthouse. Public
Records Order, Oct 23, 2007, Martin. There are no other cases, opinions, or statutory guidance
on what exactly security measures are.

Upon reviewing the record here, recognizing both that the law favors disclosure and that
this exemption, if applicable, is still conditional and can be overridden by the public interest in
disclosure, it is essentially an answer to a question from the Board regarding the integrity of local
elections. The record does not discuss, reveal, or otherwise identify any security measures or
weaknesses in security measures pertaining to the local election system even indirectly as the
courthouse video would have done. Rather, it discusses the local process, how it differs from the
State’s system, and the integrity of the local process. Additionally, because my interpretation on
review is required to favor disclosure and because of the public interest in election integrity
(both generally and currently), any arguable interpretation of the record that it could potentially
reveal weaknesses of security measures is/would be outweighed by the public interest in
disclosure.
In short, based on my review of the record and the limited interpretations of ORS
192.345(23) available, ORS 192.345(23) is not applicable to the record at issue here. Therefore,
Courier’s petition is granted, and County should disclose the record discussed above.
Respectfully,
Josh Eastman
District Attorney

Grants Pass, OR 97526
541-474-5200 | da@josephinecounty.gov
Scott Stoddard, Editor

409 S.E. 7th Street
Grants Pass, OR 97528
541.474.3726
news12@thedailycourier.com
Grants Pass Police Department Records
Attn : Captain Jim Hamilton
726 NE 7th Street
Grants Pass, OR 97526
541.450.6260
records@grantspassoregon.gov
RE: Petition for Review of Fee/Fee Waiver Re: Redwood Sign Accident dated December 22, 2021.
Dear Mr. Stoddard and Captain Hamilton/Records,
Please let this letter serve as my order regarding Mr. Stoddard’s (“Courier”) petition for
review of the fee/fee waiver regarding the video of the Redwood Sign accident pursuant to ORS
192.324(6). Since originally requested review, the Courier has since paid the fee, obtained a
copy of the video, and it is currently available for the public to view online.1 Grants Pass Police
Department Records (“City”) required an $85.00 fee for a copy of the video.
ORS 192.324(6) states that:
A requestor who believes that there has been an unreasonable denial of a fee waiver or
fee reduction may petition the Attorney General or the district attorney in the same
manner as a requestor who petitions when inspection of a public record is denied under
ORS 192.311 to ORS 192.478. The Attorney general, the district attorney and the court
have the same authority in instances when a fee waiver or reduction is denied as when
inspection of a public record is denied.
1 https://youtu.be/FaJ_qVAdukQ

ORS 192.324(4)(a) states that:
The public body may establish fees reasonably calculated to reimburse the public body
for the public body’s actual cost of making public records available, including costs for
summarizing, compiling or tailoring the public records, either in organization or media, to
meet the request.
ORS 192.324(7) requires the public body to make the fees/process for obtaining public records
written and publicly available. City’s fee schedule is online. 2
Lastly, ORS 192.324(5) authorizes a public body to “furnish copies [of the record] without
charge or a substantially reduced fee if the custodian determines that the waiver or reduction of
fees is in the public interest because making the record available primarily benefits the general
public.” (emphasis added). In other words, if the record disclosure is in the public interest, a
denial of a waiver/reduction must be “reasonable under the totality of the circumstances” which
includes the:
1) Character of the public interest in particular disclosure;
2) Extent to which fee impedes public interest; and,
3) Extent to which a waiver would burden the public body.
Public Records Order, Sept. 10, 2009, Rogers, at 3; See also In Defense of Animals v. OHSU, 199
Or App 160 (2005). In short, the first question is: does the record primarily benefit the general
public? And only if “yes,” was the denial of a waiver/reduction of the fee reasonable under the
totality of circumstances?
As relevant here, Body Worn and City Camera Video is a minimum fee of $85.00, which,
after speaking with Captain Hamilton, is based on “comparable” fees from around the state, and
is an amount approved by the City Council. The estimated fee relayed to Courier in this instance
was the minimum $85.00 fee. Courier has since paid the fee and obtained a copy of the video.
However, Courier is still seeking review of the waiver/reduction denial because Courier feels that
“the requested record falls squarely in the public interest for disclosure without an associated
fee” because it was a high-visibility news event “and the preservation of the Redwood Empire
sign is of immense public interest.”
2 (https://www.grantspassoregon.gov/DocumentCenter/View/2739/Comprehensive-Fee-Schedule---effective-8-21-
2021PDF?bidId=).

In In Defense of Animals, the Oregon Court of Appeals—as a matter of first impression—
stated that:
A matter or action is commonly understood to be ‘in the public interest’ when it affects
the community or society as a whole, in contrast to a concern or interest of a private
individual or entity.” See Black's Law Dictionary 1266 (8th ed. 2004) (defining “public
interest” as the “general welfare of the public that warrants recognition and protection”
and as “[s]omething in which the public as a whole has a stake; esp., an interest that
justifies governmental regulation”); cf. State v. Durbin, 335 Or. 183, 63 P.3d 576
(2003) (referring to the public interest in the observance of the law and the
administration of justice); Oregonian Publishing, 329 Or. at 402, 987 P.2d
480 (determining, for the purpose of a statutory exemption from disclosure of public
records, that a report resulting from an investigation of alleged misappropriation of
public property pertained to “a matter of paramount public interest and concern”); City
of Portland, 163 Or.App. at 554, 988 P.2d 402 (concluding, in context of asserted
exemption from disclosure of records pertaining to disciplinary investigation of police
officer, that “[t]he public has a legitimate interest” in determining an officer's integrity
and ability to enforce the law evenhandedly).
In addition, a matter or action “primarily benefits the general public,” as provided in ORS
192.440(4), when its most important or significant utility or advantage accrues to the
public. See Webster's at 204, 1800 (defining the verb “benefit” in part as to be useful to,
aid, advance, or improve; defining the adverb “primarily” in part as “first of all,
fundamentally, principally”; and defining the adjective “primary” in part as “first in order”
and “first in rank or importance”).
In Defense of Animals, 199 Or App at 188-189.
Here, Courier appears to conflate “public interest” – as outlined above—with the public’s
interest. That is, public oversight of governmental functions, police disciplinary investigations,
and misappropriation of public property are examples of the former whereas the sign, what
happened to it, and video of the incident are currently in the public’s interest—a current event.
That is, “public interest” is a term of art and does not cover all events the public is currently
interested in.
A previous Attorney General Opinion clarifies this distinction and informs my decision
here. In denying a fee waiver request for ODOT Records (VW/Audi Owners), it stated that:
[t]he argument for fee waiver is strongest when disclosure will inform the public about
the functioning of Oregon government. But the records here will not reveal anything
about ODOT’s operation, or the operation of any other state or local body. Your request
appears to be intended to help you contact Volkswagen and Audi owners to talk to them

about the recent emissions scandal. In addition, the $105.43 fee likely will not impede
your access to these records (and, in fact, you have already paid the fee and received the
records).
(emphasis added). Public Records Order, Oct. 18, 2016, Harden, at 3.
Similarly, here, the record involved has no relation to the functioning of local, County, or
State government. It only would provide the public with a video of a car accident that impacted
a “well-known”/famous sign in Grants Pass. 3 As such, it is more akin to a record in the interest
of “public curiosity” rather than “something in which the public at whole has a stake.” In
Defense of Animals, 199 Or App 188-189. Therefore, the minimum fee of $85.00 (which Courier
has already paid) does not impede the public interest.
In sum, City’s denial of the fee waiver/reduction here was not unreasonable under a
totality of the circumstances considering the “public interest” involved.
Respectfully,
Josh Eastman
District Attorney
3 It is also unclear whether the record would have been conditionally exempt from disclosure at this time under
ORS 192.345(3) if the driver was cited as that subsection exempts investigatory information compiled for criminal
law purposes and unclear whether “violation” / traffic citation would qualify.

title: Oregon DA Public Records Order — Fitzgerald-Clackamas Co Sheriff (Clackamas County)
text:
February 22, 2022
Brian Patrick Fitzgerald
11590 SE Aerie Crescent Rd.
Happy Valley, OR 97086
Stephen Madkour
Office of County Counsel
2051 Kaen Road
Oregon City, OR 97045
Via Email: SMadkour@co.clackamas.or.us
RE: Petition by Brian Fitzgerald for fee waiver as it relates to his public records request for “all
email, phone, and written records of Mark Shull and Paul Savas concerning Brian Patrick
Fitzgerald, from 19 OCT through 23 OCT 2021.”
Dear Mr. Fitzgerald and Mr. Madkour,
After a review of the original Fee Waiver Request to the Clackamas County Sheriff’s
office made on January 7, 202[2] and Clackamas County’s original fee estimate dated January
12, 2022, Mr. Fitzgerald’s petition for a fee waiver is denied. The order of the Clackamas County
District Attorney (CCDA) is that the fee waiver denial was reasonable because Petitioner did not
indicate how the requested records would be a benefit to the public interest.
Background
On January 7, 2022, Petitioner drafted a public records request and addressed the request
to Clackamas County Commissioner Mark Shull and Paul Savas. His request was as follows:
“All email, phone, and written records of Mark Shull and Paul Savas concerning Brian Patrick
Fitzgerald, from 19 OCT through 23 OCT 2021.” Petitioner further stated, “Thank you for
meeting this request. As a citizen journalist I expect all labor and materials be provided free of
[charge], as my investigation is in the public interest.” On January 12, 2022, Stephen Madkour,
County Counsel for Clackamas County, provided a fee estimate of at least $250 for the request.
On February 1, 2022, Petitioner appealed the denial of the fee waiver to CCDA. In his appeal,
Petitioner wrote, “This information is in the public interest. I would like the information free of
charge, as it is a serious topic. Information was obtained illegally.” On February 21, 2022,
Petitioner drafted an email to Chair Tootie Smith. In that email, Petitioner advised that he was
appealing the fee waiver denial.
Discussion
At issue here is whether Clackamas County’s denial of Mr. Fitzgerald’s fee waiver
request was reasonable under ORS 192.324. ORS 192.324(5) allows the custodian of a public
record to waive or reduce the fee associated with a public records request if disclosure of the
record at issue “… primarily benefits the general public.” Waiving or reducing fees is in the
public interest “when the furnishing of the record has utility—indeed, its greatest utility—to the

community or society as a whole.”1 The custodian of the record may deny a request for a full or
partial fee waiver even if disclosure would primarily benefit the public, provided that the denial
is reasonable under the totality of the circumstances.2
Waiving or reducing fees in the public interest is distinct from situations where disclosure
would primarily affect a concern or interest of a private individual.3 Even if the records are of a
matter which the public may generally be interested in, if the requester fails to demonstrate the
ability to meaningfully disseminate the information, disclosure will not primarily benefit the
public.4 Relevant factors to consider when determining whether a requester has established a
sufficient public interest include: (1) the requester’s identity, (2) the purpose for which the
requester intends to use the information, (3) the character of the information, (4) whether the
requested information is already in the public domain, and (5) whether the requester can
demonstrate the ability to disseminate the information to the public.5
In reviewing the non-exclusive factors listed above, the totality of the circumstances
support a finding that the fee waiver denial by the Clackamas County’s was reasonable. In Mr.
Fitzgerald’s Public Records Request, he wrote, “As a citizen journalist I expect all labor and
materials be provided free of [charge], as my investigation is in the public interest.” Mr.
Fitzgerald has provided no explanation of how the furnishing the emails would have utility to the
community or society as a whole. While Mr. Fitzgerald holds himself out as a citizen journalist
with the ability to disseminate the emails to the public, he has failed to show how these emails
would benefit the public. Although Mr. Fitzgerald alleges that certain information was obtained
illegally, with the present information, it appears these records would only be of a concern to Mr.
Fitzgerald himself.6
Order
Accordingly, Mr. Fitzgerald’s petition for a fee waiver is denied.
Sincerely,
Torrey L. McConnell, OSB # 174084
Deputy District Attorney
tmcconnell@clackamas.or.us
1 In Def. of Animals v. Or. Health Scis. Univ., 199 Or App 160, 189(2005).
2 ORS 192.324(6); In Def. of Animals v. Or. Health Scis. Univ., 199 Or App 160, 189-90 (2005).
3 Id. at 188; Public Records Order, Dec 5, 2016, DeMartino (no public interest in fee waiver where requester sought
records related to a court case he was a party to).
4 See Judicial Watch, Inc. v. Rossotti, 326 F3d 1309 (DC Cir 2003) (contrasting sufficient and insufficient
demonstrations of ability to disseminate information to public).
5 See State of Oregon, Department of Justice, Atty. Gen. Public Records and Meetings Manual, 24 (2019) (listing
factors typically considered when weighing whether the requester has established a sufficient public interest).
6 See Conklin v. United States, 654 F Supp 1104, 1106 (D Colo 1987) (finding that if a requester seeks records
relating to the requester, a mere allegation that the public body has treated the individual oppressively, absent a
broader public interest, does not satisfy the public interest standard).

title: Oregon DA Public Records Order — Watson (Josephine County)
text:
OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT ATTORNEY
Joshua J. Eastman, District Attorney
March 16, 2021
Josephine County Courthouse
Debra Watson 500 NW 6th Street, Dept. 16
3325 Cloverlawn Dr Grants Pass, OR 97526
Grants Pass, OR 97527 541-474-5200 | da@josephinecounty.gov
541.787.9708
jocofascists@gmail.com
Mark O. Stevenson
Director, Josephine County Community Development
700 NW Dimmick St., Ste. C
Grants Pass, OR 97527
541.474.5405
buildingsafety@josephinecounty.gov
RE: Pet. for Rev. of Pub. Rec. Re: 3325 Cloverlawn Request dated March 2 and March 9, 2021
Dear Ms. Watson and Mr. Stevenson,
Please let this letter serve as my order regarding Debra Watson’s (“Watson”) petition for
the disclosure of records to Josephine County (“County”) in regard to “[a]ll Sheriffs [sic], Animal
Control, code enforcement, complaints or other records pertaining to 3325 Cloverlawn Dr.
Grants Pass, OR 97527” under ORS 192.415(a). I misread the initial petition for review email (to
DA email) and did not take it as such until the follow up email on March 9, 2021.
In Oregon, “[e]very person has the right to inspect any public record of a public body in
this state except as expressly provided by ORS 192.338, 192.345, and 192.355. ORS 192.314. A
public body includes every county and city governing body,” a public record “includes any writing
that contains information relating to the conduct of the public’s business,” and a [w]riting means
handwriting, printing, photographing, and every means of recording. ORS 192.311(4-5).
Oregon Public Records Law is primarily a disclosure law, not a confidentiality law. See
Guard Publishing Co. v. Lane Co. Sch. Dist. No. 4J, 310 Or 32 (1990). Importantly, every public
record of a public body is subject to inspection, except as provided by the exemptions
mentioned above. See ORS 192.314(1). In short, the presumption is disclosure, and the
exemptions are viewed narrowly. Id. (“if there is a plausible construction of a statute favoring
disclosure of records that is the construction that prevails”).

In this instance, we are dealing with one subset of “records” that County did not disclose
to Watson when it provided the rest of the requested records to Watson. County cited ORS
192.355(4) as the exemption that precluded disclosure of the remaining records.
Watson requests that that I “stand up for [their] rights as citizens and tell Josephine
County Code Enforcement, Community Development, Animal Control, and The Sheriff that they
need to release all records including confidential complaints, video, pictures and any written
records regarding our property at 3325 Cloverlawn Dr.” However, my role in these matters is
extremely limited. It is solely to analyze the record(s) in question and “determine if it may be
withheld from public inspection.” See ORS 192.411 (in context of Attorney General) and ORS
192.415 (District Attorney as “Attorney General” role in non “state” records).
As part of the ORS 192.415 process, I have reviewed the record(s) that were disclosed to
me in this matter. Importantly, “[d]isclosure of a record to the district attorney in compliance
with subsection (1) of this section does not waive any privilege or claim of privilege regarding the
record or its contents.” ORS 192.415(3).
As mentioned above, County’s only claimed exemption is ORS 192.355(4). ORS
192.355(4) exempts from public record information that was submitted to the public agency in
confidence and whether this exemption applies is a five-part test:
1. Was the information submitted voluntarily when the informant is under no legal
obligation, statute, rule, etc. to provide the information?
2. Can County show that the “information was of a nature which reasonably should be kept
confidential”?
3. Can County show that it has obliged itself in good faith not to disclose the information?
4. Would disclosure harm the public interest?
5. Was the information, in fact submitted in confidence?
Gray vs. Salem-Keizer School Dist., 139 Or App 556, 563 (1996). All five must be present for
County to “justify non-disclosure.” Id.
In regard to No. 1, the information was on its face submitted voluntarily. The informant
had no legal obligation, no contractual obligation, nor did any statute or administrative rule

require informant to provide the information. See Guard Publ’g Co v. Lane Co. Sch. Dist. No. 4J,
96 Or App 463, 467-68 (1989).
In regard to No. 2, County has shown that the information is the type that should be kept
confidential. Doing otherwise would have a chilling effect on informant’s providing information
or coming forward and more importantly, disclosure is “restricted by statute.” See Hood
Technology Corp vs. Oregon Occupational Safety & Health Div., 168 Or App 293, 306 (2000); see
also OEC 510(2) (ORS 40.275) (“A unit of government has a privilege to refuse to disclose the
identity of a person who has furnished information relating to or assisting in an investigation of a
possible violation of law to a law enforcement officer or member of a legislative committee or its
staff conducting an investigation”).
In regard to Nos. 3 and 5, which are closely related, the evidence shows that the
information was provided on the condition of anonymity, and in exchange for the information
and the ability to obtain further information, County agreed to keep the information and the
informant confidential. There is no formal or written documentation of the agreement regarding
confidentiality, but there is an understanding between the informant and County that County
would not disclose the information—or source of information, which is all that is required. See
Public Records Order, April 5, 2002, Meadowbrook, at 6-7.
In regard to No. 4, disclosure would harm the public interest. The information
provided—and the ability of County to obtain further information were, on their face, made in
good faith. “Where a complainant has acted in good faith, disclosure is contrary to the public
interest.” Hood Technology Corp., 168 Or App at 306.
In sum, from the information provided, the nature of the records themselves, and the
above analysis, the subset of records County did not disclose are exempt from disclosure under
ORS 192.355(4) as outlined above.
Watson’s petition is denied.
Respectfully,
Josh Eastman
District Attorney

Re: Public Records Appeal
Mr. Decker and Mr. Miller,
This letter will constitute the District Attorney's order in this matter.
On December 12, 2022, Mr. Decker submitted a public records request to the City of
Eugene, as described below:
All complaints submitted to the Eugene Police Auditor or the Eugene Police
Department alleging racial profiling, biased-based policing, disparate treatment,
or a violation of Police Standards of Conduct 103.5.8(c) or 103.5.9(b)
a. Scope: All complaints that did not result in discipline
b. Timeframe: Calendar years 2019, 2020, and 2021
c. Please include
1. Source of complaint ( community member, Police
Department employee, or Police Auditor)
11. Date complaint submitted (intake date)

request
1v. Officer names and DPSST numbers for all allegations
within the scope of this request
v. Summary of incident (if not included in other documents)

review, or allegation)

v111. All allegations investigated

x. Adjudication memos

x1. Final decision for each complaint (e.g., not sustained,
exonerated, sustained, unfounded)
On March 7, 2023, the City denied the request, citing ORS 192.355(9) and ORS
181A674(3). Mr. Decker has appealed the denial.
ORS 181A.674(3) provides:
A public body may not disclose information about a personnel investigation of a
public safety employee ... if the investigation does not result in discipline of the
employee.
ORS 181A.674(4) provides that the prohibition of (3) does not apply:
(a) When the public interest requires disclosure.
ORS 18 lA.674 is not part of Oregon's public records law. It is a prohibition on
disclosure. Mr. Decker's request is specifically for complaints that did not result in
discipline. Thus, ORS 181 A.674 prohibits the disclosure of the documents, unless the
public interest requires disclosure.
Mr. Decker asserts that the public has a general interest in complaints against the police,
and how those complaints are investigated. However, such a general public interest
cannot be sufficient to overcome the prohibition against disclosure. To do so would
render the statute meaningless. lt is clear that showing must be made that the public
interest exists in a particular circumstance.
Therefore, the appeal is denied.

title: Oregon DA Public Records Order — Andersson-Clackamas County Commissioners (Clackamas County)
text:
June 10, 2021
John Andersson
Petitioner
Via Email: Stellabridge1967@gmail.com
Gary Schmidt
Clackamas County Administrator
Clackamas County
2051 Kaen Road, Oregon City, OR 97045
Via Email: GSchmidt@clackamas.us
RE: Petition by John Andersson for fee waiver as it relates to his public records request for
Clackamas County Commissioners to disclose all records regarding John Andersson’s ADA
Grievance Complaint Hearing with Clackamas County.
Dear Mr. Andersson and Mr. Schmidt,
After a review of the original Fee Waiver Request to the Clackamas County
Commissioners and Clackamas County Administrator Gary Schmidt’s original denial of the Fee
Waiver, Mr. Andersson’s petition for a fee waiver is denied. The order of the Clackamas County
District Attorney is that the Fee Waiver denial was reasonable because petitioner did not
indicate how the requested records—beyond what is already available to the public online—
would be a benefit to the public interest.
Background
On April 7, 2021, John Andersson submitted a handwritten Public Records Request to
Clackamas County, which requested “John Andersson ADA Grievance Complaint [ineligible],
Complete Record of ADA Assessment from Clackamas County Greivance [sic] complaint,
Johndeere gator, any and all records pertaining to this complaint and desisions [sic] from
county commissioners, pitchers [sic] dates [sic] from June of 2020 to April 5th 2021, all
information about this assessment, complaint, hearings, decisions, interoffice memos, video CD
from March 3, 2021 ADA [ineligible], video from Feb 3 ADA hearing.” The Public Records
Request form provided a box to check if the request primarily benefitted the general public, in
support of furnishing the records at a reduced fee or without charge. Mr. Andersson checked
this box and further stated, “This is for the benefit of the peopel [sic] so ADA laws can be
enforced and used to protect the disabled public.”

On April 12, 2021, Nathan Boderman, Assistant County Counsel for Clackamas County,
acknowledged the public records request and confirmed that the request for a fee waiver had
been sent to the County Administrator.
On April 15, 2021, Mr. Boderman emailed Mr. Andersson and alerted him that his
request for fee waiver had been denied by the County Administrator. In that same email, Mr.
Boderman provided website links to the records of the requested hearings and video recordings
of the requested hearings. Mr. Boderman clarified that an additional hearing recording would
be available within a week. Mr. Boderman offered to copy the recordings of the hearings to a
CD for no charge. With regards to the remainder of Mr. Andersson’s request for an email search
and document review from County Counsel to the extent of Mr. Andersson’s request for all
correspondence from County staff related to the matter, Mr. Boderman provided a fee
estimate of five hours of staff time at a rate of $120 per hour, which totaled $600.
On April 21, 2021, Mr. Andersson emailed Gary Schmidt directly and inquired as to the
details of Mr. Schmidt's decision to deny the request for fee waiver. On April 23, 2021, Mr.
Schmidt responded to Mr. Andersson by email with the following explanation:
Thank you for your message. When presented with a request to waive or reduce fees
associated with a public records request I employ the public interest test set forth in
statute, which provides for a waiver or reduction of fees if it “is in the public interest
because making the records available primarily benefits the general public.” This is
distinct from situations where disclosure would primarily affect “a concern or interest of
a private individual or entity.”
Based on your request and your explanation, I found that the waiver or reduction in the
cost of county staff time to respond to your public records was not in the public interest
as it did not have utility to the community or society as a whole. I use both my sound
professional judgment as well as Oregon’s public records law when I make these
determinations.
On Wednesday, June 2, 2021, Mr. Andersson appealed Mr. Schmidt’s denial of Fee Waiver to
the Clackamas County District Attorney.
/////
/////
/////

Discussion
At issue here is whether Clackamas County Administrator Gary Schmidt’s denial of Mr.
Andersson’s Fee Waiver request was reasonable under ORS 192.324. ORS 192.324(5) allows the
custodian of a public record to waive or reduce the fee associated with a public records request
if disclosure of the record at issue “… primarily benefits the general public.” Waiving or
reducing fees is in the public interest “when the furnishing of the record has utility—indeed, its
greatest utility—to the community or society as a whole.”1 The custodian of the record may
deny a request for a full or partial fee waiver even if disclosure would primarily benefit the
public, provided that the denial is reasonable under the totality of the circumstances.2
Waiving or reducing fees in the public interest is distinct from situations where
disclosure would primarily affect a concern or interest of a private individual. 3 Even if the
records are of a matter which the public may generally be interested in, if the requester fails to
demonstrate the ability to meaningfully disseminate the information, disclosure will not
primarily benefit the public.4 Relevant factors to consider when determining whether a
requester has established a sufficient public interest include: (1) the requester’s identity, (2) the
purpose for which the requester intends to use the information, (3) the character of the
information, (4) whether the requested information is already in the public domain, and (5)
whether the requester can demonstrate the ability to disseminate the information to the
public.5
In this Fee Waiver petition, Mr. Andersson originally requested the waiver on the basis
that disclosure of the records was “for the benefit of the peopel [sic] so ADA laws can be
enforced and used to protect the disabled public.” In Mr. Andersson’s petition to the Clackamas
County District Attorney, he further stated that disclosure of the hearings records would be
good for the “public interest for the disabled persons” because it would provide “a complete
record of how the hearings were held and how the information was obtained to deny the
federal law.”
/////
1 In Def. of Animals v. Or. Health Scis. Univ., 199 Or App 160, 189(2005).
2 ORS 192.324(6); In Def. of Animals v. Or. Health Scis. Univ., 199 Or App 160, 189-90 (2005).
3 Id. at 188; Public Records Order, Dec 5, 2016, DeMartino (no public interest in fee waiver where requester sought
records related to a court case he was a party to).
4 See Judicial Watch, Inc. v. Rossotti, 326 F3d 1309 (DC Cir 2003) (contrasting sufficient and insufficient
demonstrations of ability to disseminate information to public).
5 See State of Oregon, Department of Justice, Atty. Gen. Public Records and Meetings Manual, 24 (2019) (listing
factors typically considered when weighing whether the requester has established a sufficient public interest).

In reviewing the non-exclusive factors listed above, the totality of the circumstances
support a finding that the fee waiver denial by County Administrator Gary Schmidt was
reasonable. First, Mr. Andersson is requesting records specific to a grievance complaint in
which he is a party. Mr. Andersson does not provide any information to support how records
pertaining to his individual ADA hearing have a broader public interest.6 He does not provide
any information on how he intends to use the information to “protect the disabled public,” as
opposed to using the information for his own benefit. While Mr. Andersson contended a
benefit is “so ADA laws can be enforced,” he did not provide any explanation of how the
records will aid the public’s review of ADA law enforcement beyond how the ADA law was
applied to Mr. Andersson’s specific complaint. Additionally, Mr. Andersson provided no
explanation of his ability to disseminate the information to the public. Finally, a factor that
weighs against disclosure being in the public interest is the amount of records already available
to the public regarding this matter. The record from the proceeding that Mr. Andersson
references, as well as video from the hearings, are available online. Mr. Andersson does not
explain why the records already available online to the general public are insufficient for the
disabled public to evaluate Clackamas County’s application of ADA laws.
Order
Accordingly, Mr. Andersson’s petition for a fee waiver is denied.
Dated this 10th day of June, 2021.
Torrey L McConnell, OSB #174084
tmcconnell@clackamas.us
Deputy District Attorney
6 See Conklin v. United States, 654 F Supp 1104, 1106 (D Colo 1987) (finding that if a requester seeks records
relating to the requester, a mere allegation that the public body has treated the individual oppressively, absent a
broader public interest, does not satisfy the public interest standard).

RE: Petition for Review of Public Records Request denied June 15, 2020
Dear Mr. Larsen and Mr. Bartholomew,
Please let this letter serve as my order regarding Douglas Sullivan’s (“Sullivan”) petition
for the disclosure of records to the City of Grants Pass (“City”) under ORS 192.415(a). There is
no pending criminal investigation or charges.
In Oregon, “[e]very person has the right to inspect any public record of a public body in
this state except as expressly provided by ORS 192.338, 192.345, and 192.355. ORS 192.314. A
public body includes every county and city governing body,” a public record “includes any writing
that contains information relating to the conduct of the public’s business,” and a [w]riting means
handwriting, printing, photographing, and every means of recording. ORS 192.311(4-5).
Oregon Public Records Law is primarily a disclosure law, not a confidentiality law. See
Guard Publishing Co. v. Lane Co. Sch. Dist No. 4J, 310 Or 32 (1990). Importantly, every public
record of a public body is subject to inspection, except as provided by the exemptions
mentioned above. See ORS 192.314(1). In short, the presumption is disclosure and the
exemptions are viewed narrowly. Id. (“if there is a plausible construction of a statute favoring
disclosure of records that is the construction that prevails”).

In this instance, we are dealing with one “record” that consists of body camera footage
from four officers and City cites one exemption that applies under ORS 192.345(40), which is a
conditional exemption.
Because of the nature of the records, the nature of the denial, and the issue in this case, I
did not review the record as part of the ORS 192.415(3) process because the sole issue is: what is
the “public interest?”
Here, with the backdrop of no criminal case or investigation pending in mind and the
presumption favoring disclosure, my analysis is limited to whether there is a competing private
interest that, when balanced against the public interest, prohibits disclosure. See ACLU v. City of
Eugene, 360 Or 269, 292 (2016).
“Public interest” includes “transparency of police department” as well as “transparency
of government operations.” Id. In essence, a review of the applicable cases, shows that the
general “transparency of government” is a “public interest” and disclosure is favored absent an
overwhelming competing interest in nondisclosure. See e.g. City of Portland v. Bartlett, 304 Or
App 580 (2020) (even attorney-client privilege records (that were 25 years old) were subject to
disclosure).
Here, the only plausible competing interest would be privacy, but that is already
accounted for by ORS 192.345(40)(c). Therefore, the public interest in transparency of
government operations without an overriding competing interest necessitates disclosure.
City should disclose the body camera footage in accordance with ORS 192.345(40).
Respectfully,
Josh Eastman
District Attorney

Eugene, OR 97402

City of Eugene
City Attorney's Office

Re: Public Record Appeal
Ms. Flores and Mr. Miller,
This letter will constitute the District Attorney's order in this matter.
Ms. Flores made a public records request to the City of Eugene for body worn camera
videos for Eugene Police event ID number 22-221991.
The City denied the request, citing ORS 192.345(4 0). Ms. Flores filed this appeal.
Disclosure of BWC records is specifically governed by ORS 192.345(4 0). That statute
renders the recording "conditionally exempt. That is, the recording is exempt from
disclosure, "unless the public interest requires disclosure in the particular circumstance."
This determination is not one-sided. Rather, it is a balancing of the "public interest"
against the interest that is intended to be protected by non-disclosure. Further, this
balancing must be conducted under the overall umbrella of the presumption of disclosure.
This office commonly encounters a similar test in ruling on appeals concerning
"information of a personal nature." ORS 192.355(2)(a). Most significantly, what the two
tests share in common is that the interest served by disclosure must be a "public" interest.
I solicited a response from Ms. Flores identifying such an interest. Ms. Flores identified
a number of valid interests, but in my view, these are not "public" interests that would be
served by disclosure in this particular circumstance. The interest in disclosure must be
more than just a general assertion that the disclosure will benefit the public. Such an
interpretation would create a wholesale exemption to confidentiality that would render
the exemption to disclosure moot.

Therefore, the appeal is denied.
Sincerely,
PAT RICIA W. PERLOW, District Attorney
Deputy District Attorney

title: Oregon DA Public Records Order — Ausland (Josephine County)
text:
OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT ATTORNEY
Joshua J. Eastman, District Attorney
Josephine County Courthouse
April 22, 2020 500 NW 6th Street, Dept. 16
Grants Pass, OR 97526
Jack Orchard I
541-474-5200 da@josephinecounty.gov
Ball Janik, LLP
101 SW Main Street
Portland, OR 97204
503.944.6026
jorchard@balljanik.com
Mark S. Bartholomew
Hornecker Cowling LLP
14 N Central Ave, Suite 104
Medford, OR 97501
541.779.8900
Msb@roguelaw.com
RE: Petition for Review of Public Records Request denied February 21, 2020, March 13, 2020,
and April 13, 2020.
Dear Mr. Orchard and Mr. Bartholomew,
Please let this letter serve as my order regarding Jennifer Ausland's ("Ausland") petition
for the disclosure of records to the City of Grants Pass ("City") under ORS 192.415(a). The nature
of this request and the contentious backdrop in which it occurred led to a different posturing
than is typical. Ausland's request included background from Ausland's position; City's
clarification based on my follow-up email also contained background information, which was
met with an additional response arguing Ausland's position. I appreciate the contentiousness on
this issue and the detailed responses/arguments, but my role is rather limited under ORS
192.415. That is, does an exemption apply?
In Oregon, "[e]very person has the right to inspect any public record of a public body in
this state except as expressly provided by ORS 192.338, 192.345, and 192.355. ORS 192.314. A
public body includes every county and city governing body," a public record "includes any writing
that contains information relating to the conduct of the public's business," and a [w]riting means
handwriting, printing, photographing, and every means of recording. ORS 192.311(4-5}.

Oregon Public Records Law is primarily a disclosure law, not a confidentiality law. See
Guard Publishing Co. v. Lane Co. Sch. Dist No. 41, 310 Or 32 (1990). Importantly, every public
record of a public body is subject to inspection, except as provided by the exemptions
mentioned above. See ORS 192.314(1). In short, the presumption is disclosure and the
exemptions are viewed narrowly. Id. ("if there is a plausible construction of a statute favoring
disclosure of records that is the construction that prevails").
In addition to the above, ORS 192.650(2) and ORS 192.660 authorize prohibiting the
disclosure of records/executive session material "[i]f the disclosure of certain material is
inconsistent with the purpose for which a meeting ... is authorized to be held." See ORS
192.650(2); ORS 192.660.
In this instance, we are dealing with one record, which "is a PowerPoint file that was
presented in executive session." See Bartholomew's email, April 13, 2020. In City's initial denial
to Ausland's request, City stated it is "withholding one power point presentation that was
presented in executive session under various statutory authorities (ORS 192.345(1), 192.355(1),
ORS 192.660(2)(e),(f), and (h)." See Bartholomew's email-February 21, 2020.
As part of the ORS 192.415 process, I have reviewed the record that City provided to me
in this matter. Importantly, "[d]isclosure of a record to the district attorney in compliance with
subsection (1) of this section does not waive any privilege or claim of privilege regarding the
record or its contents." ORS 192.415(3).
In this case, City cites three statutory exemptions to disclosure of the record that I will
address in turn.
First, City cites ORS 192. 345(1)-the litigation exemption-which exempts from
disclosure, "unless the public interest requires disclosure in the particular instance, [r]ecords of a
public body pertaining to litigation to which the public body is a party if the complaint has been
filed, or if the complaint has not been filed, if the public body shows that such litigation is
reasonably likely to occur." ORS 192.345. This exemption is not applicable to the record in this
case. While City may have anticipated litigation would ensue at some point in the future, the
PowerPoint "did not contain information compiled because 'litigation [was] reasonably likely to

occur" and at the time it was created/utilized, "no ongoing litigation was involved." See Lane Co
School Dist No. 41 v. Parks, 55 Or App 416 (1981).
Second, City cites ORS 192.355{1), which exempts: "[c]ommunications within a public
body or between public bodies of an advisory nature to the extent that they cover other than
purely factual materials and are preliminary to any final agency determination of policy or
action" if City can show that "the public interest encouraging frank communication between
officials and employees of the public bodies clearly outweighs the public interest in disclosure."
ORS 192.355(1).
In regards the balancing test outlined in ORS 192.355{1), "the policy that permeates the
disclosure statutes and legislative history is that disclosure decisions should be based on
balancing those public interests that favor disclosure of governmental records against those
public interest that favor governmental confidentiality, with the presumption always being in
favor of disclosure." See Turner v. Reed, 22 Or App 177, 187 (1975) (emphasis added); see also
Coos Co. v. ODFW, 86 Or App 168, 172 (1987). That presumption is a difficult hurdle to clear. A
"high profile [officer involved shooting]" and the potential chilling effect of employees'
supervisor evaluations being made public were not exempt. See City of Portland v. Oregon Pub
Co, 200 Or App 120 (2005). Operating room study notes/recommendations to Hospital were not
exempt because "the public interest in frank peer review of the hospital operating rooms [does
not] outweigh[] the public's interest in disclosure." Bay Area Health Dist. v. Griffin, 73 Or App
294, 300 (1985). However, prison psychological notes and reports were exempt because
release/disclosure would have a chilling effect on candor. Turner, 22 Or App at 177 (1975).
Here, the record was undoubtedly within the public body, undoubtedly advisory in
nature, and it was preliminary to a final agency determination (well before 2020 proceedings),
and, from my review of the PowerPoint, the PowerPoint does "cover other than purely factual
materials." However, based on the policy presuming disclosure, the PowerPoint remaining
confidential does not clearly outweigh the public interest in disclosure-at least under the
traditional ORS 192.355(1) rubric. That is, there is no risk of a chilling effect, a lack of candor,
and it is important for there to be public oversight of City's spending decisions. The only risk

disclosure presents- and which City mentioned- is addressed in more detail below regarding
ORS 192.660. In short, ORS 192.355(1) is not applicable to the PowerPoint in this case.
Lastly, City cites ORS 192.660(2){e}(f), and {h) as reasons for not disclosing the
PowerPoint. For reasons discussed above regarding ORS 192.345(1), ORS 192.660(h) is
inapplicable because the PowerPoint was not created "to consult with counsel concerning the
legal rights and duties of a public body with regard to current litigation or litigation likely to be
filed." ORS 192.660 (emphasis added). For reasons discussed above regarding ORS 192.355(1),
192.660(f) is also not applicable because, from my review, the PowerPoint is not a record that is
"exempt by law from public inspection."
This leaves ORS 192.660(2)(e), which is applicable to the executive session and the
PowerPoint in this case. ORS 192.660(e) allows for City to "conduct deliberations with persons
designated by the governing body to negotiate real property transactions." This exemption only
covers "deliberations concerning negotiations on specific real property transactions." The
Honorable Carl Hosticka, Or Op Atty Gen OP-6376 (1990). This exemption is akin to ORS
192.345(6) and both exist "to permit public bodies to protect their negotiating position in real
property transactions by keeping certain information confidential." Id. (emphasis added).
Here, the PowerPoint is covered by ORS 192.660(2)(e) because it relates to City's position
in an ongoing real property transaction, which despite the presumption of disclosure that
permeates public records, is specifically authorized to remain confidential. In sum, there are two
competing public interests at play-public oversight of public bodies and fiscal prudence of
public bodies. ORS 192.660(2)(e) specifically prioritizes the latter-at least until the real estate
transaction is no longer "ongoing." Here, the transaction is stitl ongoing and therefore, ORS
192.660(2)(e) is still applicable.
II
II
II
II

In conclusion, because the real estate transaction is still "ongoing" and because of the
public interest in City maintaining its negotiating position in said real property transaction, ORS
192.660(2)(e) applies to the PowerPoint and Ausland's petition is denied.
Respectfully,
